Grant recognition & support

CEIQ Employability Grant

This study was supported by a CEIQ Employability Grant at RMIT University for the project AI-Enhanced Feedback Model for Complex Course Assignment. The project develops a feedback approach for CIVE1184 Hydrogeology, connecting disciplinary reasoning, student agency and educator oversight.

Explore the grant-supported design ↗

01 / The teaching challenge

From a collection of data
to a defensible explanation.

A groundwater model is more than a diagram. Students must connect bore logs, water levels, flow patterns and water quality—and explain why their interpretation makes sense.

That integration is where feedback matters. A plausible drawing can conceal an unsupported boundary condition, an inconsistent flow direction or an assumption that has never been tested.

With reported Hydrogeology enrolment growing from 42 in 2024 to 92 in 2026, the CEIQ project addressed a practical question: how can students receive useful, discipline-specific feedback while they still have time to act?

Enrolment describes the teaching context; it does not measure an AI effect.
01

Feedback before submission

Make revision possible while students are still building their explanation.

02

Questions about reasoning

Focus on evidence, boundaries, assumptions and consistency—not polished wording alone.

03

Students remain authors

Students evaluate advice and justify changes. Educators retain responsibility for judgement.

02 / The innovation

A feedback loop,
not an answer machine.

The project designed two connected uses of AI: formative support for student drafts and draft summative comments for educator review. The available student evaluation concerns the pilot; it does not verify deployment of every planned component.

STAGE AStudent-facing pilot

Feedback to think with

  1. Make an interpretationStudents develop a conceptual model from hydrogeological evidence.
  2. Interrogate the modelAI prompts direct attention to assumptions, flow logic, boundaries and diagram–text consistency.
  3. Check and reviseThe intended learning process asks students to check advice against course materials, calculations and educator guidance.
STAGE BDesigned educator-review pathway

Feedback under human review

  1. Draft commentsAI supports the preparation of feedback on complex submissions.
  2. Educator checks and refinesTeachers evaluate accuracy, relevance and consistency with assessment expectations.
  3. Professional responsibilityThe design retains educator oversight. Realised marking-time savings have not been established.
↳

What makes the design distinctive? It brings AI into a specific engineering reasoning task. The educational value sought is students’ ability to evaluate evidence and feedback, rather than simply obtain more comments.

See a better
feedback conversation.

Explore how a question can open up reasoning. This is an authored illustration of the intended pedagogy, not a recording of the pilot tool or a live AI service.

The student does the checking.
The student explains the revision.
ILLUSTRATIVE DRAFT CLAIM

“Groundwater flows toward the river.”

A FEEDBACK QUESTION

Which water-level measurements support that direction, and are their elevations referenced consistently?

STUDENT’S NEXT MOVE

Check the hydraulic-head evidence and datum, compare it with the arrows, then explain the support for the chosen direction.

04 / The evidence

Promising signals.
A clear-eyed evaluation.

The pilot produced useful evidence about acceptability and design. The available records do not establish that AI caused improvements in learning, marks or staff efficiency.

Students saw potential.
They also showed us what to change.

The GPT-form survey had 12 respondents; four reported that their group used the assistant. The general form had 10 respondents. Unique groups, overlap between forms and response rates are unknown.

3 of 4

respondents reporting group use supported future use

75% of this small subgroup—not a cohort estimate

AI-specific perceptions among respondents reporting use

Each row has four responses. Favourable = agree or strongly agree.

Favourable Neutral
WHAT THE EVALUATION REVEALED

Usefulness is only part of the story.

One respondent reported potentially unclear, incomplete or incorrect advice; one did not; two were unsure.

Comments called for earlier introduction and preventing offers to write report text. These are concrete design lessons about access and authorship.

Recommendations are proposed refinements, not verified implemented changes.

Confidence increased in both survey forms

Mean recalled before/after confidence: 2.50 → 3.92 on the GPT form (n=12), and 3.10 → 4.40 on the general form (n=10). Both ratings were collected after the assignment. They are retrospective perceptions, not a prospective baseline or evidence of AI causation.

Institutional course evidence

A broader practice of responsive, applied teaching

CES course base: 16/92 responses (17.4%), institutionally classified as sufficient. Individual teaching: 16 responses. Course satisfaction was 3.93 in 2024 and 4.30 in 2025; changing voluntary response sets limit comparisons.

The wider practice includes scaffolded tutorials, field learning, practitioner perspectives and in-semester student feedback. A departmental Best Early Career Teacher award also recognised S1 2026 teaching.

05 / Reflect, refine, repeat

The evaluation
is part of the innovation.

The next version should improve the learning process as well as the tool. These priorities follow from the pilot evidence and the questions it leaves open.

01 / ACCESS

Introduce it earlier.

Build onboarding into the assignment launch, demonstrate useful questions and make access expectations clear.

Proposed refinement
02 / AUTHORSHIP

Ask, don’t ghostwrite.

Tighten prompts around critique and evidence-checking. Avoid offers to generate submission-ready report paragraphs.

Proposed refinement
03 / EVALUATION

Measure the reasoning.

Use draft-to-final rubric evidence, documented exposure and comparable assessment conditions. Record staff time if efficiency is claimed.

Next-study priority
THE TRANSFERABLE INSIGHT

The question is not just whether students receive feedback.
It is whether they can judge it, use it and explain their decisions.

06 / Take the idea into your teaching

Start with a reasoning task.
Build a feedback process.

The approach can inform other complex assessment tasks. Transfer to other courses remains a proposition to evaluate, not a claim of established adoption.

  1. Name the difficult judgement.What evidence must the learner interpret, connect or challenge?
  2. Make the feedback disciplinary.Turn criteria into questions about assumptions, evidence and consistency.
  3. Require a student response.Ask what advice was accepted, rejected or checked—and why.
  4. Keep human accountability visible.Clarify educator review and authorship expectations before use.
ILLUSTRATIVE PROMPT PATTERN

Review the reasoning in this draft against the assessment criteria. Identify an unsupported assumption, an evidence gap, or an inconsistency. Ask questions that help the student investigate it. Do not write submission-ready paragraphs. Explain what the student should verify with course materials or educator guidance.

An example for adaptation, not the verified production prompt. A prompt alone does not guarantee accuracy or integrity.
